item.title: Scholarships Visiting Professorships in the Humanities These professorships are aimed at Portuguese higher education institutions seeking to host visiting professors from international universities with a distinguished academic record and recognised expertise in the field of the Humanities. closes 30 Sep 2026 Open call
item.description:
The Gulbenkian Visiting Professorships in the Humanities aim to strengthen the quality and internationalisation of teaching and research in Portugal by hosting distinguished foreign scholars. These grants target senior researchers with a well-established scientific track record, encouraging their temporary integration into Portuguese higher education institutions.

Conditions

The scholarship includes the following support:

  • Monthly stipend: €4,000
  • One-time allowance for travel and relocation: €4,000

Visits must last between 3 and 9 months and should begin within 12 months of the selection confirmation.

Eligibility

Only Portuguese Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) are eligible, and the proposed academic activities must take place in Portugal.

Applications must be submitted by the professor responsible for coordinating the visit, on behalf of the Portuguese HEI. The visiting professor is not eligible to apply directly.

How to Apply

  • The application is made by submitting an online form in Portuguese.
  • Please refer to the requirements of the call available in the document zone and check all eligibility criteria before submitting the application form.
  • To access the application form, you must first register on the website.
  • Complete all required fields to submit your application, including uploading the documentation required by the requirements of the call.
  • Submit your application some time before the deadline to avoid potential difficulties.

Results

  • Arlene Holmes-Henderson. Home Institution: Durham University. Host Institution: University of Lisbon.
  • Luca Illetterati. Home Institution: University of Padua, Host Institution. University of Coimbra.
  • Agostino Cera. Home Institution: University of Ferrara, Host Institution. University of Minho.

Contacts

E-mail: [email protected]

item.title: Film / Talks Purple Rain (1984) 27 Sep 2026 / 16:00
item.description:
The film follows The Kid, a talented young man who uses music to escape his abusive situation at home. A member of the band The Revolution, The Kid is the star of the most famous and disputed club in Minneapolis.

When he meets singer Apollonia, The Kid fights not to repeat his father’s abusive patterns, while struggling to keep together his band, threatened by rival musician Morris Day, who wants to take his place.

Part autobiographical, Purple Rain was made to promote the eponymous album, which propelled Prince to the peak of his career: with 25 million copies sold worldwide, it became one of the best-selling albums of all time.

Don’t Look Back

This event is part of the film cycle “Don’t Look Back”, which includes six documentaries and film-concerts.

item.title: Film / Film-Concert / Talks Summer of Soul (2021) 26 Sep 2026 / 16:00
item.description:
The six-week festival took place at Mount Morris Park (today Marcus Garvey Park), in Harlem, New York City, and featured big names such as Stevie Wonder, Nina Simone, Sly and the Family Stone and B.B. King, amongst others.

Commonly known as the Black Woodstock, the Harlem Cultural Festival drew a crowd of 100 thousand people, although this historic achievement had been erased from the collective memory for almost 50 years.

Registered by Hal Tulchin, the nearly 40-hour footage were archived until they were rescued by the director Ahmir Khalib Thompson. The film was officially launched in 2021 at the Sundance Festival and received several awards, including an Oscar.  

Don’t Look Back

This event is part of the film cycle “Don’t Look Back”, which includes six documentaries and film-concerts.

item.title: Concert Tchaikovsky’s Serenade for Strings 24 Sep 2026 / 20:00
item.description:
• Gulbenkian Orchestra

    In 1962, the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation decided to establish a permanent orchestral ensemble. Originally with only twelve musicians (strings and continuo) it was named “Orquestra de Câmara Gulbenkian”. This collective was successively enlarged and today the “Orquestra Gulbenkian” (the name it has adopted since 1971) has a permanent body of sixty instrumentalists, a number that can be expanded depending on the repertoire.

    This structure allows the Gulbenkian Orchestra to interpret works from the Baroque and Classical periods, a significant part of 19th century orchestral literature and much of the music of the 20th century, including works belonging to the current repertoire of the traditional symphonic orchestras. In each season, the orchestra performs on a regular series of concerts at the Gulbenkian Grand Auditorium in Lisbon, where it has had the opportunity of working together with some of leading names of the world of music (conductors and soloists). It has also performed on numerous locations all over Portugal, in an effort to decentralize music and culture.

    The orchestra has been constantly expanding its activities in the international level, performing in Europe, Asia Africa, and the Americas. In the recording field, Orquestra Gulbenkian is associated to labels as Philips, Deutsche Grammophon, Hyperion, Teldec, Erato, Adès, Nimbus, Lyrinx, Naïve and Pentatone, among others, and this activity was recognized with several international prizes.

    Hannu Lintu is the Music Director of the Gulbenkian Orchestra since 2023.

item.title: Film / Film-Concert / Talks The Last Waltz (1978) 20 Sep 2026 / 17:00
item.description:
Advertised as a farewell concert, the show attracted an audience of 5000 people and brought together several special guests, such as Bob Dylan (who refused to be filmed until the last minute,  ser filmado até ao último minuto, putting the project’s funding at risk), Eric Clapton, Neil Diamond, Emmylou Harris, Joni Mitchell, Van Morrison and Neil Young, among others.

The concert was filmed by director Martin Scorsese, who transformed it in a 116 minute documentary, considered one of the best film-concerts of all time.

The film includes live performances, interrupted by studio sessions and interviews with musicians Rick Danko, Levon Helm, Garth Hudson, Richard Manuel and Robbie Robertson, who reflect on the history of the band and life on tour. 

Don’t Look Back

This event is part of the film cycle “Don’t Look Back”, which includes six documentaries and film-concerts.

item.title: Film / Film-Concert / Talks Stop Making Sense (1984) 20 Sep 2026 / 20:00
item.description:
Jonathan Demme follows the band at the height of their career, creating an immersive experience for the audience. The film starts with singer David Byrne alone on the stage, which takes shape gradually as the other elements are brought together.

Filmed during the course of three nights, the documentary includes the band’s first hits, like Psycho Killer, the latest singles at the time, as well as songs from the singer’s solo repertoire and from the Tom Tom Club project, by drummer Chris Frantz and bassist Tina Weymouth.  

Hailed by critics as one of the best concert films ever made, Stop Making Sense is an essential film for Talking Heads fans, offering a glimpse into the New Wave scene of the late 1970s and early 1980s.

Don’t Look Back

This event is part of the film cycle “Don’t Look Back”, which includes six documentaries and film-concerts.

item.title: Film / Talks A Hard Day’s Night (1964) 19 Sep 2026 / 17:00
item.description:
The first Beatles feature film follows the four members of the mythical band, who are preparing for a televised concert, while dealing with a strict manager, hysterical fans ans problematic relatives.

The musicians portray over-the-top comical versions of themselves, recording a period that forever changed the history of music. The soundtrack is taken from the eponymous album, A Hard Day’s Night, edited in 1964.

Filmed during Bob Dylan’s famous transitional period to rock and the electrical guitar, this documentary follows the musician from his arrival in England, on April 26th 1965, and the last concert of the tour at the Royal Albert Hall, on May 10th.

The director had access to the backstage, offering a glimpse into Dylan’s public and private life, from concerts to hotel room conversations, recording his tumultuous relationship with singer-songwriter Joan Baez during a critical phase of his musical career.

A number of well-known figures are featured in the film: Dylan’s agents Albert Grossman and Bob Neuwirth, musicians Donovan, Joan Baez, Marianne Faithfull and Alan Price (Animals), and the beat poet, Dylan’s close friend, Allan Ginsberg, among others.

Don’t Look Back

This event is part of the film cycle “Don’t Look Back”, which includes six documentaries and film-concerts.

Missa Utica by Sammy Baloji is a performance that revisits the early contacts between Europe and the Kingdom of Kongo, intertwining colonial memory, spirituality, and music.

In partnership with Contemporânea, the CAM presents, at the intersection of live performance, concert, and artistic montage, Missa Utica (2024) by Sammy Baloji (DR Congo, 1978). The work brings together performers Fiston Mwanza Mujila, Pytshens Kambilo, and Barbara Drazkow Drążkowska in a dialogue with the historical ties between Europe and the Kingdom of Kongo. Memories of colonisation interweave with spirituality, colonial memory, music, and performance.

Based on extensive research conducted by Sammy Baloji on Congolese objects scattered across European collections, Missa Utica returns to the initial contact between Western Christianity and the Central African region, which occurred around the final years of the 15th century. Episodes linked to the evangelical religious conversion of the Kingdom of Kongo, colonial power dynamics, and the resulting cultural and political transformations are revisited within this context.

The title refers to Utica, an ancient Roman city located within the borders of modern-day Tunisia—a place chosen as a symbol, as it was there that the first African bishop of Black descent, Dom Henrique, son of King Afonso I of Kongo, was consecrated. This historical moment serves as a starting point to reflect on how European Christianity spread across the African continent and the relationships it forged with slavery, colonisation, and processes of cultural erasure.

A key highlight of the work is the Missa Luba, a liturgical composition created in the Belgian Congo in the 1950s by Franciscan missionaries, based on traditional Congolese musical styles. Although it gained visibility in Europe and the United States, little was said about the colonial conditions that allowed for its emergence. In Missa Utica, this past resurfaces, but now intertwined with Congolese rumba, recited verses, and improvised sounds.

Throughout the performance, music, text, and image merge into layers; different temporalities occupy the same space without hierarchy. Bodies speak for themselves, bringing forward histories of displacement, resistance, and survival. Voices emerge as traces of struggle and persistence against erasure. In this way, memory does not remain solely in the past—it reappears.

Rather than committing to a single format, Missa Utica blends elements of modern ritual with traces of sound performance. The work follows Sammy Baloji’s ongoing investigation into how colonial archives shape identities, historical narratives, and collective imaginaries.

Missa Utica is part of the Performance Program My Center is Not in the Solar System, under the artistic direction of Celina Brás and curated by Alexandra Balona.

item.title: Grants Gulbenkian Energy Communities Supporting renewable energy community projects in Portugal that empower citizens to play an active role in the energy transition. closes 16 Sep 2026 Open call
item.description:
Since Portugal introduced its first legal framework for collective self-consumption of renewable energy in 2019, community-led renewable energy initiatives driven by citizens, associations and local authorities have gradually begun to emerge.

Although Renewable Energy Communities (RECs) offer significant environmental, economic and social benefits, fewer than ten are currently operating in Portugal. RECs enable citizens to come together to generate, share, consume and store renewable energy, creating value both for their members and for the communities in which they operate.

In response to the absence of dedicated public funding for citizen-led Renewable Energy Communities, the Gulbenkian Foundation has partnered with Coopérnico – Sustainable Development Cooperative to support civil society organisations working alongside citizens, local authorities and other local stakeholders.

The initiative seeks to address some of the key barriers to establishing Renewable Energy Communities, including the upfront investment required to launch projects, limited technical capacity within local organisations and communities, and low levels of energy literacy among citizens.

Through this call, the Gulbenkian Foundation expects to fund 10 projects, with grants of up to €30,000 each.

Objectives

Grant funding will be awarded to projects that contribute to:

  • expanding decentralised renewable energy generation and local energy use;
  • strengthening the involvement of local authorities, community organisations and cooperatives in community energy initiatives;
  • promoting collective action through participatory governance models;
  • increasing the participation of economically vulnerable citizens and households;
  • encouraging Renewable Energy Communities in rural and low-density areas, while promoting greater territorial diversity;
  • fostering diversity and representation in project leadership and coordination.

Application process

The call for proposals will take place in two stages.

  • In the first stage, between 14 July and 16 September 2026, applicants are invited to submit an Expression of Interest outlining their proposal to establish a Renewable Energy Community, assessed on the basis of the proposed project and the profile of the lead organisation. The 20 highest-ranked applications will progress to the second stage.
  • In the second stage, between 19 and 30 October, the organisations behind the 20 shortlisted proposals will take part in a two-week online capacity-building programme. Following this programme, and based on the development of the proposals, 10 finalist projects will be selected to receive grant funding from the Gulbenkian Foundation.

Webinar

A webinar to present the call and answer questions will take place on 21 July, from 17:30 to 18:30, with prior registration required, including an open Q&A session.

Conditions

  • Grants are available only to legal entities established and registered in Portugal.
  • The amount awarded to each project will be determined during the final selection process and will not exceed €30,000.
  • Eligible costs include: administrative expenses associated with establishing a Renewable Energy Community; licensing procedures; the purchase and installation of renewable energy generation equipment for collective self-consumption and local energy sharing.

Eligibility

Applications are open to locally based, non-profit legal entities registered in Portugal.

This call is intended to support Renewable Energy Communities at an early stage of development. Therefore, at the time of application, organisations must not have a licensing application pending or already approved by the Directorate-General for Energy and Geology in Portugal; or have received funding from any public or private organisation for projects relating to Renewable Energy Communities or collective self-consumption.

How to Apply

  • Only applications submitted online will be accepted;
  • Register at  MyGulbenkian;
  • Before submitting your application form, check all the eligibility criteria and be sure to read the Call Conditions (available in the documents section);
  • Applications may only be submitted once all the mandatory fields of the form have been completed and the documents required under the Call Conditions have been uploaded;
  • Don’t forget to click “submit application”. Try not to submit your application in the last few days leading up to the deadline to avoid any unforeseen last minute problems.

Faq

Who can apply?

This call is open to civil society organisations that represent citizens' interests, are actively engaged with their local communities, and are committed to playing an active role in the energy transition through democratic participation.

Do members of a Renewable Energy Community need to be located within the same parish or municipality?

No. Under Portuguese legislation, members do not need to be located within the same parish or municipality. However, they must be located within 2 km of the renewable energy generation system (or 4 km in low-density areas), or be connected to the same electricity substation.

Can an informal group of citizens apply?

No. The Gulbenkian Foundation provides grants only to legally established non-profit organisations. An informal group of citizens may partner with an eligible organisation whose statutory objectives are aligned with this call, but it cannot receive funding directly from the Foundation.

Can a municipality or parish council apply? What about a local energy agency or another municipal body?

No. This call is intended to support citizen-led Renewable Energy Communities (RECs), meaning communities led by organisations representing groups of citizens, such as associations or cooperatives.

Municipalities, Parish Councils, local energy agencies and other municipal bodies may participate as project partners, but they cannot lead, manage or submit an application.

Is a recently established association, cooperative, foundation or other non-profit organisation eligible?

Yes.

Can an organisation submit more than one application?

No. Each organisation may submit only one application.

Are partnerships required?

No. However, partnerships formally confirmed through Letters of Support submitted with the application may strengthen the quality and feasibility of the proposal.

Are project partners required to make a financial contribution?

No. Partners may contribute in other ways, for example by making rooftops or other suitable spaces available for the installation of photovoltaic panels.

Can a research centre established as a non-profit private legal entity apply?

No. This call is not intended to fund research projects.

Can projects involve partnerships with for-profit organisations?

Yes. Projects may include local businesses or service providers with a relevant role in the community, provided that their participation falls within the scope of their corporate social responsibility activities rather than constituting a commercial service.

These organisations cannot become the sole owners of the project assets. Ownership must be shared.

Will certain territories be given priority?

Yes. Preference will be given to applications from low-density areas or territories facing greater social, economic or environmental vulnerabilities. Applicants should explain and justify these circumstances in their proposal.

Can an organisation that is already receiving funding from the Gulbenkian Foundation apply?

Yes. However, priority will be given to organisations that have never received, or are not currently receiving, funding from the Foundation. Projects that are already being funded by another public or private organisation will not be eligible for support.

Can the grant be used to recruit staff?

No.

What are the requirements for successful applicants?

In addition to managing the grant in accordance with the Foundation's funding rules, successful applicants must participate in all activities organised as part of this initiative, including the capacity-building programme delivered by Coopérnico.

They will also be required to submit a progress report after the start of the project and a final report, using templates provided by the Foundation.

Will there be an information session?

Yes. A free online webinar will take place on 21 July 2026, from 17:30 to 18:30 (Lisbon time). 

Can a national or regional organisation submit a project with a local focus?

Yes, provided that the proposal clearly demonstrates its local relevance.

Can project partners be changed after the application has been approved?

Yes, provided that the change does not compromise the objectives or successful implementation of the project.

Do the future members of the Renewable Energy Community need to be identified in the application?

Applicants should identify the prospective members of the Renewable Energy Community.

Can an organisation with no previous experience in the energy sector apply?

Yes. This call is intended for organisations that consume electricity, not for organisations already operating in the energy sector.

Should the project be selected, the organisation will need to amend its statutes in order to establish a Renewable Energy Community. The costs associated with this process are eligible for funding under the grant.

Can organisations based in the Autonomous Regions of the Azores and Madeira apply?

Yes. Organisations based in the Autonomous Regions are fully eligible to apply.

The only difference concerns the competent licensing authority. In mainland Portugal, the registration, prior control and licensing of Renewable Energy Communities are carried out by the Directorate-General for Energy and Geology (DGEG). In the Autonomous Regions, these responsibilities lie with the Regional Directorate for Energy (DRE) in the Azores and the Regional Directorate for Energy and Climate Change (or Regional Directorate for Energy) in Madeira.

What is meant by "vulnerable citizens or households" for the purposes of this call?

For the purposes of this call, vulnerable citizens or households are those experiencing financial hardship and at risk of energy poverty, as demonstrated by their eligibility for, or receipt of, the Social Electricity Tariff or the Social Natural Gas Tariff.

The aim is to support households for whom energy costs represent a significant financial burden and who stand to benefit most from the cost savings associated with participation in a Renewable Energy Community.

Does an REC have to be based on photovoltaic solar energy?

No. A Renewable Energy Community (REC) may choose other renewable energy generation systems. However, within the scope of this call, only solar photovoltaic generation systems will be considered, as they are currently the most cost-effective technology and the quickest to license and install.

Can a condominium (residential building or multi-family building) apply?

No. A condominium is not eligible because it does not constitute a formally established civil society organization.

Contacts

Questions about this call should be sent to: [email protected].

Before contacting us, please read the Call Conditions carefully and consult the Frequently Asked Questions, as your query may already be answered there.

item.title: Concert Quatuor Diotima 12 Sep 2026 / 19:00
item.description:
Event Slider

Date

  • 19:00 / Cancelled 19:00 / Sold out Saturday, 19:00

Location

Pricing

Ticket collection, subject to room capacity (max. 2 per person):

In-person – 2 hours before
Online – 2 days before (Cartão Gulbenkian Mais) and 1 day before (Cartão Gulbenkian), from 10:00.

  • Quatuor Diotima
  • Yunpeng Zhao Violin
  • Léo Marillier Violin
  • Franck Chevalier Viola
  • Alexis Descharmes Cello

Betsy Jolas

Béla Bartók

Maurice Ravel

György Kurtág

The Diotima Quartet is one of the most acclaimed string quartets of today, its name deriving both from the female character created by Hölderlin in the novel Hyperion and from a landmark string quartet piece by Luigi Nono. Its reputation for excellence has been built through close collaboration with Pierre Boulez and Helmut Lachenmann, as well as performances of works by Beethoven, Schubert, Ravel and Bartók. The Diotima joins the Kurtág / Jolas Cycle at Gulbenkian in a programme bringing together works by the two celebrated composers alongside pieces by Ravel and Bartók.

Photo © Michel Nguyen

Sponsor Gulbenkian Music

item.title: Concert A Little Summer Suite 11 Sep 2026 / 19:00
item.description:
• Gulbenkian Orchestra

    In 1962, the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation decided to establish a permanent orchestral ensemble. Originally with only twelve musicians (strings and continuo) it was named “Orquestra de Câmara Gulbenkian”. This collective was successively enlarged and today the “Orquestra Gulbenkian” (the name it has adopted since 1971) has a permanent body of sixty instrumentalists, a number that can be expanded depending on the repertoire.

    This structure allows the Gulbenkian Orchestra to interpret works from the Baroque and Classical periods, a significant part of 19th century orchestral literature and much of the music of the 20th century, including works belonging to the current repertoire of the traditional symphonic orchestras. In each season, the orchestra performs on a regular series of concerts at the Gulbenkian Grand Auditorium in Lisbon, where it has had the opportunity of working together with some of leading names of the world of music (conductors and soloists). It has also performed on numerous locations all over Portugal, in an effort to decentralize music and culture.

    The orchestra has been constantly expanding its activities in the international level, performing in Europe, Asia Africa, and the Americas. In the recording field, Orquestra Gulbenkian is associated to labels as Philips, Deutsche Grammophon, Hyperion, Teldec, Erato, Adès, Nimbus, Lyrinx, Naïve and Pentatone, among others, and this activity was recognized with several international prizes.

    Hannu Lintu is the Music Director of the Gulbenkian Orchestra since 2023.

• Marisol Montalvo

    Soprano

    The American soprano is among the most sought-after exponents of contemporary music working today. She is possessed of an extraordinarily flexible instrument, “brilliantly stratospheric” yet “sweet-voiced”, that has enabled her to achieve success in repertoire from Strauss to Boulez. A consummate, “unstinting” singing actress, she has been greatly acclaimed for identifying unconditionally with her characters.

    As well as performing alongside many of the world’s most renowned conductors and orchestras, she has had the privilege of working closely with many of today’s leading composers, including Matthias Pintscher, Olga Neuwirth, and Wolfgang Rihm. Several have written roles especially for her, including Peter Eötvos (Sierve Maria in Love and Other Demons), Pascal Dusapin (Prothoe in Penthesilea) and Marco Stroppa (Olbia in Il Re Orso). Her affinity for contemporary music has led to regular engagements with ensembles including Klangforum Wien, Ensemble Intercontemporain, International Contemporary Ensemble (ICE), Ensemble Remix and Ensemble Modern.

    Although she has achieved success in a wide range of operatic repertoire, Montalvo is particularly associated with the title role of Berg’s Lulu. Following her debut in the part at the Opéra National de Paris, Le Monde described her performance as a true revelation: “The American soprano possesses real stage and vocal presence, and executes the exhausting role with incredible intensity”. Subsequently, Lulu has become the centerpiece of her stage work; she has performed it at houses including Deutsche Oper Berlin, Théâtre du Capitole Toulouse, Teatro de la Maestranza, Theater an der Wien, Komische Oper Berlin, and at Theater Basel, in the acclaimed production by Calixto Bieto.

    Outside the opera house, Montalvo has a particularly close working relationship with Christoph Eschenbach, who has been both a mentor and a regular concert partner throughout her career. Since conducting her Carnegie Hall debut with the Philadelphia Orchestra, he has invited her to work with him alongside orchestras including the Vienna Philharmonic, the Houston Symphony, the London Philharmonic, the Munich Philharmonic and the Orchestre de Paris. Most recently, she performed the role of Sophie in a concert performance of Der Rosenkavalier with the National Symphony Orchestra under his baton at the Kennedy Center in Washington, DC.

    She has also worked with conductors including Daniel Harding, Vladimir Jurowski, Christopher Hogwood, Yuri Temirkanov, Bernhard Kontarsky, Sylvain Camberling, Sussana Mälkki, Lothar Zagrosek, and Sir Neville Marriner, and with orchestras including the Cleveland Orchestra, the Los Angeles Philharmonic, the San Francisco Symphony, St Petersburg Philharmonic, DSO Berlin, SWR Sinfonie-Orchestra, RSO Wien, Finnish Radio Symphony Orchestra, and the Bamberger Symphoniker. She has performed at houses including Opernhaus Zürich, Bregenzer Festspiele, Gran Teatro del Liceu, Baden-Baden Festspielhaus, Teatro Real de Madrid, Glyndebourne Festival Opera, Theatre du Chatelet, Théatre de Geneva, La Monnaie de Munt, Opera de Monte Carlo, Lithuania National Opera, Polish National Opera and Opera Comique.

item.title: Grants Core Funding for Environmental Organisations Strengthening the capacity of organisations working to conserve nature and biodiversity. closes 07 Sep 2026 Open call
item.description:
In Portugal, more than half of all habitats are in decline. Civil society organisations working in nature conservation play a vital role in protecting biodiversity through the conservation, management and restoration of ecosystems. However, these organisations face significant funding and capacity challenges that limit the continuity and long-term impact of their work.

To help address these challenges, the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation launched the first edition of this programme in 2025, awarding core funding to eight environmental organisations. The programme demonstrated the value of core funding in strengthening organisations’ stability, independence and capacity to deliver lasting impact.

With this second edition, the Foundation is renewing its commitment to supporting organisations that play an essential role in protecting the environment and safeguarding Portugal’s natural heritage. By complementing traditional project-based grants, core funding gives organisations the flexibility to strengthen their capacity and pursue their mission in a more sustainable and effective way.

Conditions

  • Financial support will only be awarded to legally established entities registered in Portugal;
  • The amount of each grant will be determined during the final selection process and will not exceed €50,000.

Eligibility

Applications are open to organisations officially recognised as environmental organisations under the National Register, or equivalent organisations, as well as organisations working in the field of nature conservation whose activities align with the objectives of this call and which meet the eligibility criteria set out in the Call Conditions.

How to Apply

  • Only applications submitted online will be accepted;
  • Register at  MyGulbenkian;
  • Before submitting your application form, check all the eligibility criteria and be sure to read the Call Conditions (available in the documents section);
  • Applications may only be submitted once all the mandatory fields of the form have been completed and the documents required under the Call Conditions have been uploaded;
  • Don’t forget to click “submit application”. Try not to submit your application in the last few days leading up to the deadline to avoid any unforeseen last minute problems.

Contacts

Questions about this call should be sent to: [email protected].

item.title: Concert Vale do Silêncio 05 Sep 2026 / 21:30
item.description:
• Gulbenkian Choir

    The Gulbenkian Choir was founded in 1964 by the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation as a full symphonic body of around 100 singers. The choir joins the Orquestra Gulbenkian and other orchestras to perform Classical, Romantic and Contemporary choral-symphonic repertoire, but can also perform a cappella. It has performed – and often premiered – many 20th century works by Portuguese and international composers.

    The Gulbenkian Choir has been invited to collaborate with major international orchestras, under the direction of conductors such as Claudio Abbado, Colin Davis, John Nelson, Emmanuel Krivine, Esa-Pekka Salonen, Frans Brüggen, Franz Welser-Möst, Gerd Albrecht, Michael Gielen, Michael Tilson Thomas, Rafael Frübeck de Burgos, René Jacobs and Leonard Slatkin, among others.

    Besides its regular season of concerts in Lisbon and frequent national tours, the Gulbenkian Choir has repeatedly toured Argentina, Belgium, Brazil, Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Hungary, India, Iraq, Israel, Italy, Japan, Macao, Malta, Monaco, Netherlands, Spain, the United Kingdom, the United States of America and Uruguay.

    The Gulbenkian Choir has recorded extensively for Philips, Deutsche Grammophon, Erato, Cascavelle, Musifrance, as well as FNAC-Music, performing a wide range of repertoire, from Early-Renaissance polyphony to Xenakis. Several of these albums received international awards.

    Martina Batič is the current Principal Conductor, succeeding Michel Corboz (1969–2019), Inês Tavares Lopes the Associate Conductor and Jorge Matta the artistic consultant.

  • Gulbenkian Orchestra

    In 1962, the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation decided to establish a permanent orchestral ensemble. Originally with only twelve musicians (strings and continuo) it was named “Orquestra de Câmara Gulbenkian”. This collective was successively enlarged and today the “Orquestra Gulbenkian” (the name it has adopted since 1971) has a permanent body of sixty instrumentalists, a number that can be expanded depending on the repertoire.

    This structure allows the Gulbenkian Orchestra to interpret works from the Baroque and Classical periods, a significant part of 19th century orchestral literature and much of the music of the 20th century, including works belonging to the current repertoire of the traditional symphonic orchestras. In each season, the orchestra performs on a regular series of concerts at the Gulbenkian Grand Auditorium in Lisbon, where it has had the opportunity of working together with some of leading names of the world of music (conductors and soloists). It has also performed on numerous locations all over Portugal, in an effort to decentralize music and culture.

    The orchestra has been constantly expanding its activities in the international level, performing in Europe, Asia Africa, and the Americas. In the recording field, Orquestra Gulbenkian is associated to labels as Philips, Deutsche Grammophon, Hyperion, Teldec, Erato, Adès, Nimbus, Lyrinx, Naïve and Pentatone, among others, and this activity was recognized with several international prizes.

    Hannu Lintu is the Music Director of the Gulbenkian Orchestra since 2023.

  • Cláudia Semedo

    Apresentadora

    Cláudia Semedo é atriz e apresentadora de televisão. Nascida em Oeiras em 1983, completou o Curso de Interpretação da Escola Profissional de Teatro de Cascais em 2001 e licenciou-se em Jornalismo na Escola Superior de Comunicação Social em 2012.

    É presidente da Companhia de Atores e diretora artística do Teatro Municipal Amélia Rey Colaço, desde janeiro de 2017.

item.title: Grants Portugal + Preparado Supporting a project that contributes to developing a culture of earthquake preparedness and resilience in Portugal closes 31 Aug 2026 Open call
item.description:
Portugal faces a significant seismic risk, particularly in the Lisbon and Algarve regions. Although recent earthquakes have served as a reminder of this vulnerability, public and political responses have often remained intermittent and reactive, rather than part of a sustained, evidence-based approach to preparedness.

As part of its 70th anniversary celebrations, the Gulbenkian Foundation is launching this call to support the design and implementation of a project that brings together science, communication and public action. The initiative seeks to strengthen connections between academia, civil society and policymakers, helping to build a more informed and resilient society.

The project should contribute to improving public understanding of seismic risk, strengthening the preparedness of families, schools and organisations, and supporting more effective public policies and decision-making in the field of earthquake preparedness and resilience.

An online information session will be held on 18 June 2026 at 11:00 (Lisbon time). Enroll: [email protected]

Conditions

The maximum support available is €250,000, including taxes and any other associated costs. Projects may have a duration of up to 18 months. Proposals must not exceed 12 pages, excluding annexes.

Indicatively, proposals may address one or more of the following areas:

  • Knowledge and public policy – organisation of conferences, working groups and other initiatives that contribute to knowledge production and the development of strategic recommendations for policymakers.
  • Capacity building and awareness raising – development of educational resources, training activities, communication campaigns, earthquake drills and other initiatives aimed at schools, professionals, organisations and the general public.
  • Pilot and demonstration projects – implementation of experimental actions that test innovative approaches, generate practical evidence and support their future integration into programmes or public policies.

Eligibility

Proposals must be submitted by a single coordinating organisation with recognised scientific and technical expertise in the field of earthquakes and seismic risk.

The coordinating organisation may establish and lead a consortium with other relevant entities, while retaining overall responsibility for the strategic coherence, partnership coordination and delivery of the project.

How to Apply

  • Register to apply;
  • Before submitting the application form, check all the eligibility criteria. We advise you to read the Call Conditions (available in the Documents area, in Portuguese only)
  • Applications can only be submitted once all the mandatory fields of the form have been completed and the documentation required by the Call Conditions has been uploaded;
  • After filling the form, click on the ‘submit application’ button. In order to prevent difficulties in submitting applications, avoid submitting your application in the last few days of the deadline.

item.title: Concert Chicago Underground Duo 09 Aug 2026 / 18:30
item.description:
Event Slider

Date

  • 18:30 / Cancelled 18:30 / Sold out Sunday, 18:30

Location

Pricing

10% – Cartão Gulbenkian

  • Chad Taylor Drums, Percussion, Mbira, Kalimba
  • Rob Mazurek Trumpet, Piccolo trumpet, Electric piano, Modular synths, Samplers, Voice, Flute, Bells

Rob Mazurek and Chad Taylor ended the Chicago Underground Duo’s 11-year silence with the release on International Anthem of Hyperglyph, a feast of jazz colliding with the deconstructed language of post-rock, an African-rooted rhythmic palette and the experimental exuberance of electronics.

Their reunion follows experiences with collectives such as Exploding Star Orchestra, Fly or Die (by Jaimie Branch) and Marshall Allen’s Ghost Horizons, resulting in a dialogue that combines Taylor’s trance-like percussion with Mazurek’s constant centrifugal motion, employing a wide array of instruments and a multimedia dimension reserved for the stage.

A prodigious space between jungle and city, ancestry and future projection.

The Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation reserves the right to collect and keep records of images, sounds and voice for the diffusion and preservation of the memory of its cultural and artistic activity. For further information, please contact us through the Information Request form.

item.title: Concert SML 09 Aug 2026 / 21:30
item.description:
Event Slider

Date

  • 21:30 / Cancelled 21:30 / Sold out Sunday, 21:30

Location

Gulbenkian Garden

Pricing

10% – Cartão Gulbenkian

  • Anna Butterss Electric bass
  • Jeremiah Chiu Synthesizer, Live-Sampling, Percussion
  • Josh Johnson Saxophone, Electronics
  • Booker Stardrum Drums, Percussion
  • Gregory Uhlmann Electric guitar, Effects

When the quintet SML (Small Medium Large) – the supergroup formed by Anna Butterss, Jeremiah Chiu, Josh Johnson, Booker Stardum and Gregory Uhlmann – debuted in 2024, Pitchfork described the album as “an exciting milestone” in contemporary avant-garde music, suggesting that SML “may signal a new iteration of jazz, or it may not even be jazz, or it may not even matter”.

In SML’s music, various genres implode as they are referenced, in a voracious approach that exhausts possibilities, quickly tires of them and moves in another direction. Each instrument, as in the early electric phase of Miles Davis (2026 marks his centenary), transcends its characteristic sound and becomes a portal to another surprising dimension.

The Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation reserves the right to collect and keep records of images, sounds and voice for the diffusion and preservation of the memory of its cultural and artistic activity. For further information, please contact us through the Information Request form.

item.title: Concert Pat Thomas 08 Aug 2026 / 18:30
item.description:
Event Slider

Date

  • 18:30 / Cancelled 18:30 / Sold out Saturday, 18:30

Location

Pricing

10% – Cartão Gulbenkian

  • Pat Thomas Piano

A regular presence at Jazz em Agosto in recent years, having performed with collectives such as Ahmed, The Locals and X-Ray Hex Tet, the British musician Pat Thomas appears this time in a solo piano concert based on the album Hikmah (2025).

Hikmah, an Arabic word meaning “wisdom or knowledge”, serves as the thematic umbrella for an album that, as Marc Corrotto writes in All About Jazz, “reaffirms Pat Thomas as a singular voice in improvised music”.

“Thomas invites the listener to focus deeply, but also to let go without restraint, as if suspended between prayer and dream. His left hand often acts as an anchor, while the right ventures into the unknown.” As though the spiritual and the earthly inhabit the keys of his piano simultaneously.

The Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation reserves the right to collect and keep records of images, sounds and voice for the diffusion and preservation of the memory of its cultural and artistic activity. For further information, please contact us through the Information Request form.

item.title: Concert Tomas Fujiwara: Dream Up 08 Aug 2026 / 21:30
item.description:
Event Slider

Date

  • 21:30 / Cancelled 21:30 / Sold out Saturday, 21:30

Location

Gulbenkian Garden

Pricing

10% – Cartão Gulbenkian

  • Tomas Fujiwara Drums, Composition
  • Ches Smith Vibraphone, Percussion
  • Kaoru Watanabe Taiko drums, Japanese flutes
  • Kweku Sumbry Balafon, Ngoni, Percussion

Dream Up is the percussion quartet of Tomas Fujiwara, one of the most active, ubiquitous and creative figures in New York jazz.

A frequent collaborator of Taylor Ho Bynum, Mary Halvorson and Tomeka Reid, Fujiwara now explores a shared percussive sound with Kaoru Watanabe, Ches Smith and Kweku Sumbry, broad enough to include vibraphone, the African ngoni and the Japanese shinobue flute.

For Jazz Trail, Fujiwara’s pieces build “a bridge between Max Roach’s M’Boom percussion ensemble and the vibraphone gems recorded by Bobby Hutcherson for Blue Note in the 1960s and 70s”. The same review praises Fujiwara’s “rhythmic intelligence, dazzling virtuosity and fearless imagination”, both honouring diverse traditions and seeking an innovative perspective.

The Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation reserves the right to collect and keep records of images, sounds and voice for the diffusion and preservation of the memory of its cultural and artistic activity. For further information, please contact us through the Information Request form.

For Jazz Trail, Fujiwara’s pieces build “a bridge between Max Roach’s M’Boom percussion ensemble and the vibraphone gems recorded by Bobby Hutcherson for Blue Note in the 1960s and 70s”. The same review praises Fujiwara’s “rhythmic intelligence, dazzling virtuosity and fearless imagination”, both honouring diverse traditions and seeking an innovative perspective.

  • Nick Dunston Double bass, Electronics

Faced with the remarkable originality of the music composed by Ches Smith for the project Clone Row, Marc Ribot ventured to write that it is like “listening to a Jim Hall concert under the influence of many mushrooms” or, alternatively, “a post-punk, post-Dave Brubeck, post-trip-hop experience with classical form”.

While Ches Smith’s talent as a drummer is widely recognised (Darius Jones, John Zorn, Tim Berne and many others), Clone Row is a dazzling demonstration of his superb imagination as a composer, channelled into this formation of two guitars, bass and electronics.

Disorienting music, in which each composition explores a new angle on how to brush against the different guitar styles of Mary Halvorson and Liberty Ellman.

An explosion of ideas.

Flautist, saxophonist and composer, Anna Webber has in recent years secured a deserved and prominent place in the New York jazz scene, building a reputation as an innovative musician whose work has featured in year-end lists by outlets such as The New York Times and National Public Radio.

For this quintet, formed by other leading figures of American jazz (Adam O’Farrill, Mariel Roberts, Elias Stemeseder and Lesley Mok), Webber composed music based on an ancient tuning system rooted in natural harmonics and resonance.

According to Free Jazz Collective, “the arrangements, orchestration and performance create a sense of depth, momentum and theatricality that contributes to the narrative quality of this highly engaging music”.

item.description:

  • Mariam Rezaei Turn-table
  • Lukas König Drums, Amplified cymbal, Synthesizer

One year after their explosive appearance at Jazz em Agosto, Mariam Rezaei returns to the festival with her creative ferocity, drawing highly experimental sounds from the turntable.

The quartet, which also features Mette Rasmussen, Gabriele Mitelli and Lukas König (on saxophone, piccolo trumpet and drums respectively), takes its name from a work by Goya and treats genre demolition as a daily practice. “By integrating noise, jazz, electronic music and pure madness,” the group’s presentation states, “this quartet does not sit passively waiting for something to happen.”

Instead, surrendering to febrile improvisation, the group (whose debut album appeared in 2025) creates music that, in the words of The Wire, results in a “superb, absorbing album – reflective and creative”.

item.title: Concert Bonbon Flamme 04 Aug 2026 / 21:30
item.description:
Event Slider

  • Fulco Ottervanger Piano, Synthesizer, Voice
  • Étienne Ziemniak Drums, Electronics, Synthesizer

After an intense journey through Mexico, Valentin Ceccaldi, cellist and founder of the Bonbon Flamme collective, returned home with the desire to compose music nourished by everything he had absorbed: the vibrant colours of nature and the streets, the acidity of lemons, the sweetness of avocados, the fire of chillies, the omnipresence of violence and death, and the relationship with ancestors and religion.

All of this is present in the quartet’s second album, Calaveras y Boom Boom Chupitos. Joined by three other incendiary musicians (Luís Lopes, Etienne Ziemniak and Fulco Ottervanger), Ceccaldi leads music with “a vast palette of colours” that adds “atmospheric pieces, occasional childlike melodies and a touch of ragtime”, according to UK Jazz News.

Magnificently delirious.

  • Ricardo Marques Electric bass
  • João Sousa​ Drums

On its 20th anniversary, the project created and led by Marco Barroso brings to Jazz em Agosto a singular and irreverent vision of the big band sound.

Comprising musicians from both jazz and classical backgrounds, LUME explores the typical vocabulary of this type of ensemble while simultaneously playing with its clichés and injecting references from rock, popular music, avant-garde jazz, contemporary composed music and experimentalism.

For London Jazz News, “Marco Barroso has developed within LUME a uniquely functioning sonic organism, also evident in his minimalist conducting style”.

The starting point is always the same: to think of each composition as a space of infinite possibilities and an opportunity to point towards a different horizon.

item.description:

  • Brandon Lopez Double bass

In its selection of the ten best jazz albums of 2022, The New York Times wrote about the remarkable record by bassist Brandon López, drummer Gerald Cleaver and poet Fred Moten, noting how Moten “pursues a complete questioning of the ways in which Black knowledge systems have been exploited and discarded, yet still reborn”.

In Revision (2025), Moten once again collaborates with López, deepening the relationship between untamed word and fervent, highly visual music. Revision is music of today, conscious in its response to current political insanity and the enduring place of resistance within the African American population.

As The Quietus writes, “this is not exactly a call to arms, but rather an urgent invitation to rethink our world”.

  • Nick Jost Electric bass
  • Danny Sher Drums

Cruelty Bacchanal, writes Matt Hollenberg, “is about the erosion of empathy – about how the celebration of violence and the embrace of nihilism have become a display of strength in modern society”. This is how the leader of Shardik conceives the group’s second album for Tzadik, music made of pieces that fracture and reorganise themselves in different ways.

Blending codes from heavy metal, free jazz and classical composition, and always seeking uncharted sonic escapes, Hollenberg’s guitar joins forces with Sana Nagano’s violin, Nick Jost’s bass and Danny Sher’s drums.

According to Everything Is Noise, “vaguely Eastern European nuances” combine with a “deliberate evocation of ancient Roman festivities”, reflecting a world in convulsion – politically, humanly and socially.

  • Rodrigo Amado Tenor saxophone
  • David Maranha Electric organ

The world is not going through an easy moment. Wars, natural disasters, political extremism, totalitarian threats, volatile economies, stark inequalities, climate anxieties, hate speech and intolerance, uncertain tomorrows.

The presentation text for Wrecks, a meeting between the tenor saxophone of Rodrigo Amado and the electric organ of David Maranha, refers to this contemporary storm as the backdrop for this unsettling music woven by the two.

This context did not escape the attention of Free Jazz Blog, which accompanied a top-rated review with a description of the “industrial, violent, melody- and harmony-free” sound created by Maranha as a foundation; above it, Amado “soothes, sings, laments, howls, screams”, creating an intense soundtrack for a world in flames.

item.description:
Event Slider

  • Jerome Deupree Drums
  • Joe Morris Double bass
  • Sylvie Courvoisier Piano
  • Lester St. Louis Cello

Improvised music, in the hands of its finest practitioners, resembles a fiercely contested sporting event with an unpredictable outcome. With the original quartet Canyon, it is easy to see that anything is possible.

Drummer Jerome Deupree provided the rhythmic backbone to the alternative rock of Morphine; cellist Lester St. Louis made his name in Jamie Branch’s Fly or Die; guitarist Joe Morris is, according to The Wire, “one of the deepest improvisers active in the United States”; pianist Sylvie Courvoisier is a colossus of inventiveness, described by Deupree as someone who keeps the group “on the edge of their seats, because the piano seems unable to contain her”.

In truth, everything in Canyon is unrestrained: the energy, the sonic exploration, the four-way communication, the vibration, the urgency.

  • Joachim Kühn Piano

Clear proof of his inexhaustible creative source, Joachim Kühn recorded the double solo album Échappée for Intakt Records shortly before turning 80.

Since the 1960s, the German pianist has been one of the leading figures in avant-garde jazz, thanks to an extraordinarily rich pianistic language that draws equally from the jazz tradition and the legacy of European classical music. This free and expansive world is fully present in Échappée, with Jazzwise highlighting the coexistence of references such as Ravel, Chopin, Bud Powell and Art Tatum.

“Do not expect calm, crystalline improvisation,” Jazzwise also wrote, “but rather a frenetic gallop which, after repeated listening, reveals an underlying sense of structure beneath the apparent randomness of cascading notes.”

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
MISKOLC – Four years after one of Central Europe's most serious river pollution disasters, a cross-border investigation examines what caused the contamination, whether the river has truly recovered, and what lessons remain unanswered.

In 2022, the Sajó River, which flows from Slovakia into Hungary, became the site of one of Central Europe's most serious environmental disasters. Mine water containing arsenic and other heavy metals entered the river system, threatening ecosystems and raising concerns among communities living along its banks. Although emergency measures were introduced, many questions surrounding responsibility, transparency and the long-term environmental consequences have remained unanswered.
This cross-border investigation by Borsod24 and Parameter.sk revisits the disaster several years later to assess what has changed. Through independent laboratory testing, field reporting, interviews with experts, environmental organisations, public officials and local residents, as well as extensive document analysis, the project examines both the causes of the disaster and the current condition of the river.
Beyond reconstructing the events of 2022, the investigation explores whether institutional responses were sufficient, whether pollution risks continue to exist, and what practical measures could prevent similar environmental disasters in the future. By combining scientific evidence with human stories from both sides of the border, the project aims to strengthen public accountability and improve understanding of cross-border environmental protection.

Key Findings

  • The 2022 Sajó River contamination exposed significant weaknesses in environmental monitoring and institutional preparedness.
  • The disaster affected communities in both Slovakia and Hungary, demonstrating the cross-border nature of environmental risks.
  • Independent laboratory measurements are being used to compare current water quality with previous official data.
  • Local residents continue to raise questions regarding transparency, communication and long-term environmental impacts.
  • Experts highlight the importance of improved monitoring systems and stronger international cooperation to prevent similar incidents.

Methodology

The investigation combines documentary research, field reporting, cross-border collaboration and independent scientific verification. The reporting team analysed official documents, historical reporting, environmental data and public records, while conducting interviews with environmental experts, local residents, civil society organisations and public officials. Independent water samples were collected at multiple locations and analysed by an accredited laboratory. The results are compared with previous official measurements and interpreted with expert assistance. The project also includes on-location video reporting documenting the affected areas and the experiences of local communities.

Themes

  • Environment

Publication

ONLINE

  • A vörös folyó története: A Sajó-katasztrófa egy régió látlelete, Borsod 24, 16/07/2026
  • A vörös folyó története: A Sajó-katasztrófa egy régió látlelete, Parameter, 16/07/2026

COUNTRIES

  • Hungary
  • Slovakia

Team members

Tamás Gobodics

Tamás Gobodics is a journalist with several decades of professional experience, focusing on motorsport and public affairs.

Bálint Barak

Bálint Barak is the co-founder of Parameter.sk.

Adrián Fazekas

Adrián Fazekas is a journalist at Borsod24.

István Neumahr

item.content:encoded:
MISKOLC – Four years after one of Central Europe's most serious river pollution disasters, a cross-border investigation examines what caused the contamination, whether the river has truly recovered, and what lessons remain unanswered.

In 2022, the Sajó River, which flows from Slovakia into Hungary, became the site of one of Central Europe's most serious environmental disasters. Mine water containing arsenic and other heavy metals entered the river system, threatening ecosystems and raising concerns among communities living along its banks. Although emergency measures were introduced, many questions surrounding responsibility, transparency and the long-term environmental consequences have remained unanswered.
This cross-border investigation by Borsod24 and Parameter.sk revisits the disaster several years later to assess what has changed. Through independent laboratory testing, field reporting, interviews with experts, environmental organisations, public officials and local residents, as well as extensive document analysis, the project examines both the causes of the disaster and the current condition of the river.
Beyond reconstructing the events of 2022, the investigation explores whether institutional responses were sufficient, whether pollution risks continue to exist, and what practical measures could prevent similar environmental disasters in the future. By combining scientific evidence with human stories from both sides of the border, the project aims to strengthen public accountability and improve understanding of cross-border environmental protection.

Key Findings

  • The 2022 Sajó River contamination exposed significant weaknesses in environmental monitoring and institutional preparedness.
  • The disaster affected communities in both Slovakia and Hungary, demonstrating the cross-border nature of environmental risks.
  • Independent laboratory measurements are being used to compare current water quality with previous official data.
  • Local residents continue to raise questions regarding transparency, communication and long-term environmental impacts.
  • Experts highlight the importance of improved monitoring systems and stronger international cooperation to prevent similar incidents.

Methodology

The investigation combines documentary research, field reporting, cross-border collaboration and independent scientific verification. The reporting team analysed official documents, historical reporting, environmental data and public records, while conducting interviews with environmental experts, local residents, civil society organisations and public officials. Independent water samples were collected at multiple locations and analysed by an accredited laboratory. The results are compared with previous official measurements and interpreted with expert assistance. The project also includes on-location video reporting documenting the affected areas and the experiences of local communities.

Themes

  • Environment

Publication

item.title: Concert Orquestra Juvenil Geração 26 Jul 2026 / 18:00
item.description:
• Orquestra Juvenil Geração

    Orquestra Geração/Sistema Portugal was founded in 2007/2008 in Amadora through a partnership between the Municipality of Amadora, the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation and the Music School of the National Conservatory, inspired by Venezuela’s El Sistema.

    Over the past 18 years, Orquestra Geração has become a flagship project for social inclusion through orchestral music. Its success has been shaped by exchanges with Venezuelan teachers and conductors, the support of the Ministry of Education and the municipalities that have joined the initiative, as well as by private partners who share the conviction that music, the arts and culture are essential and irreplaceable in the full development of both societies and individuals, regardless of their backgrounds, beliefs or social circumstances.

    Today, the project reaches more than 1,700 children and young people, many of whom have gone on to pursue specialised music studies at leading institutions in Portugal and abroad.

  • Jose Jesus Olivetti

    Jose Jesus Olivetti is a young Venezuelan violinist and conductor who trained within the renowned National System of Youth and Children’s Orchestras and Choirs of Venezuela (El Sistema), where he began his musical journey at the age of eight. He studied violin with Savino D’Addona, Rubén Camacho and Francisco Díaz, and began his conducting studies with Tarcísio Barreto. He received training from Maestro José Antonio Abreu not only in orchestral conducting, but also in the design, planning and implementation of musical and orchestral projects. He later continued his studies in Europe with distinguished conductors including Jorma Panula, Colin Metters, Alex Treger and Maurice Hamers.

    Olivetti has participated in numerous international festivals and advanced training programmes, working with the Ruse Philharmonic Orchestra, the Burgas State Opera, the Berlin Philharmonic Chamber Orchestra and the Lithuanian State Symphony Orchestra.

    He has conducted major festivals and projects with Orquestra Geração in Portugal, as well as with national and international orchestras in Switzerland, Portugal, Spain and other countries. In 2023, he was among the winners of the Düsseldorf International Conducting Festival.

    As a conductor and guest conductor, he has collaborated with orchestras across the world, promoting access to classical music for international audiences.

    Alongside his artistic career, Jose Jesus Olivetti combines his musical activities with a strong social commitment. Through the Olivetti Foundation, which he founded, he develops projects aimed at supporting young talent, including the international competition Tocar y Luchar, sustainable support for orchestras in Angola and Mozambique, and specialised training programmes and lectures for musicians and educators in Medellín, Colombia.

    He also created the Meet the Community project, designed as a bridge between the orchestras he conducts, regional music schools and young musicians. The initiative promotes cultural, musical and artistic exchange, offering young people the opportunity to gain first-hand insight into the work and reality of a professional orchestra.

    Olivetti completed his studies at the Leopold Mozart College of Music of the University of Augsburg, where he studied conducting with Professor Maurice Hamers and violin with Professor Senta Kraemer. He was awarded scholarships by the Theodor Rogler Foundation in Germany and the Elena Probst Foundation in Switzerland.

    Jose Jesus Olivetti is currently Music Director of the Philludiker Orchester München, the Bodensee Ärzteorchester and the Garchinger Sinfonieorchester. He is also a violinist with the Seraphin Ensemble München and the Münchner Kammerphilharmonie Dacapo.

item.title: military families and vets
item.description:
As the son of a World War II veteran and as a teenager who grew up during Vietnam, Craig saw up close how badly returning vets were treated. It’s stayed with him throughout his life.

Craig believes we need to protect the people who protect our country. That means supporting servicemembers on our frontlines -- and their families at home. It also means helping these men and women after they retire from their service.

Those who wear the uniform too often can’t financially afford to continue their service as long as they’d like. It pisses Craig off that many of these families need help finding affordable housing, and that some even need occasional food assistance just to survive. Craig knows that these failures make our country less secure. And that they’re not fair.

Craig has donated more than $100 million to veteran groups nationally and in local communities. Through Blue Star Families and the Bob Woodruff Foundation, Craig has helped thousands of active-duty servicemembers, veterans and their families get the support they need during and after their service.

item.title: #CyberCivilDefense
item.description:
Craig grew up at a time when patriotism was a thing, encouraged by his Greatest Generation parents. In WW2, everyone was expected to help defend the country, here at home, and mostly overseas, where the fighting took place.

In the current cyber war, the fight is on our own shores, and we all need to play an active role for the protection of our country and ourselves.

Craig was part of the whole “duck and cover” thing, in the 50s and 60s, and realizes that we need civil defense in the cyber domain, “cyber civil defense.” This is patriotism, for regular people.

He's committed $100 million to form a Cyber Civil Defense network of groups who are starting to protect the country from cyber threats. Attacks on our power grids, our cyber infrastructure and even the internet-connected gadgets and appliances in our homes are real. If people think that’s alarmist, tell them to “Blame Craig.”

The core of Cyber Civil Defense includes groups like Aspen Digital, Global Cyber Alliance, and Consumer Reports, focusing on citizen cyber education and literacy, cyber tool development, and cybersecurity workforce programs aimed at diversifying the growing field. 

The effort, launched in 2022, has already made significant investments in Black Girls Hack, Girls Who Code, the Girl Scouts, VetsinTech, the Consortium of Cyberclinics, the Ransomware Task Force, and Shadowserver.

item.title: promoting the truth
O, Miami redefined what a poetry festival can be Miami 5 min read
item.description:
• Daniel Rivero

Overview

On April 22, 2014, a strangely familiar man rode a white horse down Calle Ocho, the heart of Cuban Miami. The man was an actor, hired to portray Cuban national hero and acclaimed poet José Martí. Martí died in 1898, but as his reincarnated likeness passed, helpers handed out white roses bearing his poems.

As the horse trudged on, unsuspecting elderly Cubans gathered to witness the unlikely event. Many recited lines of poetry they had learned in childhood.

“These viejitos were following us as we’re all walking down Calle Ocho. And then – my parents coming, my grandmother getting the roses. Something happened there,” says Melody Santiago Cummings, executive director of O, Miami. “I felt changed.”

Welcome to O, Miami –– possibly the world’s most inventive and dynamic poetry festival.

Seamlessly dovetailing between the whimsical and the heartfelt, the festival has become a Miami institution since it rose up from the ashes of a city that was a major epicenter of the 2008 financial crisis.

As families lost homes and businesses shuttered, the city experienced a renaissance driven by artists and visionaries eager to activate the sudden surplus of inexpensive studio space.

In 2009, Knight Foundation provided seed funding to an experimental poetry project, the University of Wynwood, the brainchild of poet and essayist P. Scott Cunningham. Three years later, Knight funded O, Miami, a citywide poetry festival, the natural outgrowth of that early experiment.

Unlike most poetry festivals, there was not one venue, one ticket, one wristband. Instead, The O, Miami festival named an impossible-sounding mission that it pursued with creativity and flair: to ensure that everyone in Miami encountered a poem during April, National Poetry Month.

All manner of poetry events have been held over the ensuing annual festivals. There have been readings by emerging and established poets, yes. But also, poetry has found itself embedded in events like a Poetry Is Dead mock funeral procession, athletic competitions, oyster tastings, underwater poetry in a hotel pool, a poetry-themed remake of 2 Fast 2 Furious and a Bad Bunny lookalike contest.

  • Photo credit: Gesi Schilling
  • Caroline Cabrera and Melody Santiago Cummings. Photo credit: Gesi Schilling.

Places where Miamians have encountered poetry:

  • Fruit stickers in supermarkets
  • Pints of ice cream
  • Girl Scout cookies
  • Freshly poured concrete sidewalks
  • Urinals
  • Miami Metrorail tickets
  • Airplane banners
  • Bus stops
  • Labels stitched into T-Shirts on store racks
  • Two rooftops visible to travelers flying in and out of Miami International Airport
  • Sandwiches
  • Beach sand

In 2019 Knight provided a major non-project grant that helped O, Miami plant deeper roots as an organization that could look towards the future. By then, the once-affordable real estate market of the festival’s early days had swelled into one of the most expensive in the nation, putting pressure on O, Miami and other cultural organizations.

“You don’t want your success to be totally reliant on one funder –– and I think we’ve been able to mature out of that –– but had it not been for Knight, we would not be here,” says Santiago Cummings.

In recent years, the festival has expanded significantly, evolving into a year-round organization. Teachers across South Florida now incorporate poetry into their classrooms using O, Miami’s Sunroom curriculum. An annual summer apprenticeship program has become an incubator for artists of all mediums. The organization regularly publishes books, ranging from poetry to prose, from quirky poetry about Miami’s weird side to children’s books and anthologies tackling transportation, climate change and gun violence.

The team has also begun to offer creative services to local governments and businesses, helping fill funding gaps while advancing its mission. Storefronts and construction sites throughout the city now routinely feature poetry written by South Florida residents.

“Our problem is that we do too much to effectively tell the story of who we are and what we do,” jokes artistic director Caroline Cabrera.

Impact at a glance

Since 2011…

  • 875 events or projects produced
  • 30 titles published
  • 2,755 Miami-Dade County students served
  • Dozens of classroom poetry anthologies distributed
  • More than 42,000 poems collected

In 2025 alone…

  • More than 150 events held in four languages
  • Eighteen artists mentored
  • 56 poems displayed on windows and storefronts
  • Thousands of books sold
  • 9,000 poetry fruit stickers placed on produce in three languages
  • 90 pounds of plastic recycled into poetry
  • 410 linear feet of poetry fences installed throughout Miami
  • 466 poems exchanged for bread

The Impact

  • 875

    Events or projects produced since 2011

  • 2,755

    Miami-Dade County students served

  • 90

    Pounds of plastic recycled into poetry in 2025

  • Photo credit: Gesi Schilling
  • Photo credit: Gesi Schilling

During April, the festival really does feel like it is everywhere. A decade-and-a-half partnership with public radio station WLRN means poems are broadcast to commuters during rush hour throughout the month. The collaboration also spawned an entirely new poetry form: the ZipOde.

In a ZipOde, the numbers in a given zip code determine the number of words in a line, and the resulting poem must be about that specific place. Public radio listeners began submitting ZipOdes in 2015; to date, more than 20,000 poems have been collected. An anthology published on the tenth anniversary of the ZipOde pairs poems collected over the years with photography.

ZipOdes have spread across the country, with versions of the poetry form and related events have popped up in Massachusetts, Ohio, Maryland and beyond.

The key to O, Miami’s success is a deeply felt love for its namesake city, in all of its diversity.

“We are a placemaking organization,” says Cabrera. “If an idea can spark a conversation about this place or lead to true moments of self-expression in this space and celebrate it in all its complexity, we will entertain it.”

Daniel Rivero is an investigative reporter with WLRN Public Radio in Miami. How work has been featured in the Miami Herald, NPR, the Guardian, ABC News and other outlets. His first book, Just Freedom: Inside Florida’s Decades-Long Voting Rights Battle, was published in 2025.

“We are a placemaking organization. If an idea can spark a conversation about this place or lead to true moments of self-expression in this space and celebrate it in all its complexity, we will entertain it.”

item.title: What it takes to paint at monumental scale, with Sydney James Detroit 5 min read
item.description:
• Ashley Simon

Overview

Sydney G. James is a Detroit-born and Detroit-based fine arts painter and muralist whose large-scale public works and studio practice explore Black identity, representation and community. She earned a BFA from the College for Creative Studies and began her career as an art director in advertising before expanding into visual art in film and television in Los Angeles. James returned to Detroit in 2011 and has since completed murals locally and across the globe, including the acclaimed Girl With the D Earring in the North End.

She was awarded a 2017 Kresge Arts in Detroit Fellowship and co-founded the BLKOUT Walls street mural festival, creating platforms for diverse artists. Her work has been exhibited at institutions including the Museum of Contemporary Art Detroit and the Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History, as well as galleries such as Detroit Artists Market, Red Bull House of Art and Janice Charach Gallery.

Q&A

When you’re starting something like this, what’s the very first thing you have to do? Where does it all begin?

The first thing I do is research. I look at the location—what it is, what it was, and how it’s structured. I ask the basic questions: who, what, where and why.

With The Girl with the D Earring, that meant really spending time in the North End. There’s a lot of history there, especially around Black life and Black presence in the neighborhood. I wanted to understand the people in the area and what that place actually is.

The building itself—the Chroma building—was originally a cold storage facility, so that history mattered too. I often use compositions that already exist in pop culture. In this case, it was The Girl with the Pearl Earring. The “D” comes from the Detroit Tigers logo, but it’s also bigger than that—it’s the branding of Detroit.

Community engagement is important to me, especially with public work. I want it to be a two-way conversation between the artist and the people who live around it. The work should feel enjoyable and relatable to the community.

When I was contacted to work on the Ralph C. Wilson site, there were a few things I had to consider right away. The structure is unique—it’s a ventilation system. It’s also owned by Canada and visible from Canada. Because of that, it couldn’t just work from one angle. It had to be a full 360 experience. You have to think about who can see it and how far away they are.

Once I do the homework, I start drawing. For Ralph C. Wilson, I listed out ideas of what people can actually do and enjoy in a public park. I wanted to draw something that works whether you’re young or old, able-bodied or disabled. And everybody can enjoy bubbles. It’s something people can experience together.

I also like to put little Easter eggs in my work. Inside the bubbles, there are small silhouettes showing different ways to get to Canada—the tunnel, the bridge. It’s a simple composition, but it says a lot. You don’t have to put the kitchen sink in there.

What tools, skills, or supports do you absolutely rely on to make this work possible?

The tools change with the job. Going back to Ralph C. Wilson, for example, you can’t do something like that alone. You need people. You need relationships—especially with lift rental companies. They come out, review the site and tell you exactly what equipment you’ll need. A lot of the time, you’re gauging a project based on what you’ve done before.

With The Girl with the D Earring, I worked with a team of six people and we finished it in about five and a half days. I thought it would be the same with Ralph C Wilson Park—ha!—but I didn’t fully account for the scale. It’s about 2000 sq ft larger than Girl with the D Earring because of the size and the 360-degree nature of it.

I also have Sherwin-Williams come out to help estimate how much paint I’m going to need. Big projects need big equipment and big tools.

Smaller projects are different. For those, I used mural paint by Chroma. It’s a more liquid outdoor–indoor acrylic with really great coverage.

No matter the tools, though, I want you to be able to recognize my work. The tools can change, but the voice should still be there.

What would you say is the most difficult part of the work that demands the most from you mentally or logistically?

It’s physical. I don’t care if you’re on a small wall or a huge wall. Mural artists aren’t blue-collar or white-collar—we’re just collared. We have to be trained on the equipment like any other construction worker. We need the same certifications and the same insurance.

It’s physically challenging, and it’s mentally challenging too, because you’re often isolated. You might be standing for hours. It’s intensive labor. That’s the part a lot of people don’t see or understand, because art is so—art is so beautiful.

What’s one mistake or failure that taught you something important or essential?

Whatever happens on this planet—good or terrible—there are lessons everywhere. With the Ralph C. Wilson Park project, I had a huge mess up with the UV protection coating . The product wasn’t mixed properly and it sprayed on very thick and uneven.. An hour later,  it rained hard. The following day, I woke up to a text from someone at the park with photos attached, asking, “Is this supposed to look like that?” It didn’t look right at all. There was a thick foggy film covering my painting; specifically the biggest face on the painting. It was so frustrating because we’d already put a lot of work in. That moment taught me patience. Step away. If you’re unsure or feeling overwhelmed, don’t come back angry. Take a beat, take care of yourself, and then come back with a solution.

How do you stay sane? What helps keep your perspective or keep you grounded when things become overwhelming?

I always remind myself that everything turns out ok. Everything is fixable. I can’t control how other people treat me or perceive me, but I can control how I respond.

What’s one book that you think everyone should read?

E.M. Forster’s science fiction short story The Machine Stops. Everybody should read it.
